A shortage: consumers demand more grain because the government subsidy makes it cheaper for them
Efficient allocation: the market clears at the government price, producing exactly the socially optimal quantity
Price discrimination: foreign buyers pay the full market price while domestic consumers pay the subsidized price
answer: Surplus production: farmers grow more at the higher price, creating stockpiles that the government must store or sell at a loss
explanation: A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus — quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded. EU and US farm price support programs historically produced 'butter mountains,' 'wine lakes,' and grain mountains. These surpluses had to be stored (costly), destroyed (politically embarrassing), or dumped on world markets at subsidized prices (harming developing-country farmers). This is a price floor in action: it benefits producers but creates waste and costs taxpayers.

prompt: When a rich-country government subsidizes its own fishing fleet, this creates an 'externality' — an external cost imposed on which parties?
choices: Foreign fishers and future generations — subsidies allow over-fishing that depletes shared fish stocks beyond sustainable levels
Domestic fish consumers — subsidies raise retail prices by supporting inefficient domestic fleets
Commercial shipbuilders — subsidized fleets reduce demand for new vessels by keeping old ones operating longer
Neighbouring countries' navies — subsidized fishing fleets expand into exclusive economic zones, creating territorial disputes
answer: Foreign fishers and future generations — subsidies allow over-fishing that depletes shared fish stocks beyond sustainable levels
explanation: Fishing subsidies (estimated at $35 billion/year globally) enable fishing beyond what the underlying fish stocks can sustain. This depletes fish stocks that are a common resource — harming foreign fishing communities that depend on the same stocks and future generations who inherit depleted oceans. It's a classic 'tragedy of the commons' problem amplified by state support. The WTO reached a historic fisheries subsidies agreement in 2022 to limit harmful subsidies for the first time.

prompt: Fishing-permit buyback schemes pay fishers to retire their boats or licences. What is the main economic rationale?
choices: To permanently cut fishing capacity by paying owners to leave, rather than relying only on catch limits that are costly to enforce and easy to evade
Fishers who are paid not to fish become advocates for conservation, influencing their communities to fish sustainably
The payment directly compensates fishers for the externality they impose on future fish stocks
International maritime law prohibits direct catch limits but allows financial incentives
answer: To permanently cut fishing capacity by paying owners to leave, rather than relying only on catch limits that are costly to enforce and easy to evade
explanation: Catch limits require monitoring, enforcement and penalties, all costly and imperfect (fishers can misreport catches). Buying out boats and permits aims to remove fishing capacity for good and reduce the pressure to overfish without constant policing; it is a Coasian approach that changes the economic incentive rather than regulating behaviour. The US, EU and Australia have all used buybacks, but results are mixed: remaining fishers may invest in better gear ('capital stuffing') and retired capacity can creep back unless entry is also restricted.

prompt: The 'Ikea effect' — named after the furniture company — describes what psychological phenomenon?
choices: People value things they built themselves more highly than identical ready-made items, proportional to the labour they invested
People are more likely to buy a product if it comes with assembly instructions, because effort creates perceived value
Consumer satisfaction with IKEA furniture increases after assembly because anticipation is more enjoyable than the product itself
People prefer difficult-to-assemble products because complexity signals quality and craftsmanship
answer: People value things they built themselves more highly than identical ready-made items, proportional to the labour they invested
explanation: Norton, Mochon, and Ariely (2012) showed that people valued their self-assembled IKEA furniture comparably to professional work — and were willing to pay far more for objects they built than for identical ready-made versions. This 'IKEA effect' is a variant of the endowment effect combined with labour justification bias. It has implications for product design (involvement increases attachment), education (struggling with problems improves learning), and investment (people overvalue stocks they researched themselves).

prompt: Microfinance — lending small amounts to poor borrowers without collateral — was celebrated as a poverty-reduction miracle in the 1990s and 2000s. Later randomized controlled trials found what surprising result?
choices: Microloans modestly raised business investment but had little measurable effect on average incomes or poverty over the longer run, so the transformative claims were overstated
Microfinance reduced poverty only for women borrowers, not for men, due to different spending patterns
Microloans were statistically shown to increase poverty by trapping borrowers in debt cycles with high interest rates
The RCTs confirmed early enthusiasts' claims: microfinance reduced poverty by 40-60% wherever it was rigorously tested
answer: Microloans modestly raised business investment but had little measurable effect on average incomes or poverty over the longer run, so the transformative claims were overstated
explanation: A series of RCTs in the 2010s (Banerjee, Duflo and others in India, plus studies in Bosnia, Ethiopia, Mexico, Mongolia and Morocco) found modest effects: microloans helped some borrowers invest in existing businesses and manage cash flow, but the large poverty-reducing effects claimed by early advocates of Yunus and the Grameen Bank did not materialize. Effects on household income, children's schooling and women's empowerment were small and inconsistent. The story shows how development economics moved from anecdote-based advocacy to rigorous measurement.
